passage:
Dear Professor Menon,

I hope this finds you well. I am writing to ask whether I might submit my literature assignment on Friday instead of Wednesday, as I have been unwell and behind on reading. I have attached what I have finished so far, and I will send the remainder as soon as I can. I understand if this is not possible, and I am grateful for your time.

With thanks and regards,
Uma

P.S. to Jaya (separate text): hey! sent the prof a mail asking for extension, wish me luck 🙂 will tell you what he says!! 🤞

Uma reread the two versions once more and thought about how her words changed when the reader changed.

qa.q: On which day did Uma ask to submit her assignment?
qa.a: She asked to submit it on Friday instead of Wednesday.

qa.q: How might Uma feel as she writes to the professor and then to Jaya?
qa.a: She is nervous and hopeful, asking Jaya to wish her luck, and she is polite and careful with the professor but relaxed with her friend.

qa.q: What could Uma do if she wanted the email to sound even more appropriate?
qa.a: She could keep it short, state clearly what she needs and by when, and leave out chatty phrases from her messages to friends.

qa.q: How might Professor Menon see the email?
qa.a: The professor may see it as respectful and clear, and likely to be taken seriously, though the decision still depends on the course rules.

grounding: Uma shifts between formal and informal register for a professor and a friend.

passage: I'm Lokesh, and I want to tell you about the worst email I ever sent. I was applying for a summer job at a print shop, and I'd typed it the way I text my friends: "hi, i saw the ad, want to join, when do i start?" No greeting, no name, nothing. My friend Baljeet read it over my shoulder and burst out laughing. "You wouldn't say that to an interviewer in person," he said. He wasn't unkind, and I got the point. I rewrote it: "Dear Ms. Kaur, I am writing to apply for the position advertised... I have attached my CV." It felt stiff, but they invited me for an interview the next day. I still keep the first draft as a reminder of how small choices change the impression.

qa.q: What kind of job was Lokesh applying for?
qa.a: Lokesh was applying for a summer job at a print shop.

qa.q: How did Lokesh feel when Baljeet laughed, and what did Lokesh take from it?
qa.a: Lokesh probably felt a bit embarrassed, but took the point that the message sounded too casual, and Baljeet's tone was not unkind.

qa.q: What did Lokesh do that worked?
qa.a: Lokesh rewrote the email with a greeting, a name, a clear purpose and an attached CV, and it led to an interview.

qa.q: How might the print shop owner have seen the first draft?
qa.a: The owner might have read it as careless or unaware of norms, though Lokesh could still have been serious, and the tone left that unclear.

grounding: Lokesh learns that a person's register should match the relationship after an overly casual job email.
